newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ car plants to hit end of line as tariffs to go.
newsitem.headline: NZ car plants to hit end of line as tariffs to go.

text.p: New Zealand's 50-year-old car assembly industry is coming to the end of the line and other sectors are threatened following a government signal it wants to abolish tariffs soon, industry commentators said on Wednesday.

Treasurer Winston Peters in Thursday's budget said New Zealand would take a global lead, and had no intention of awaiting a 2010 deadline by which APEC (Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation) forum countries had agreed to remove tariffs.
"There are no prizes for coming last," he said.

He also stressed he would not take a wait-and-see approach, announcing he was bringing forward a review of auto tarrifs due in 1998 "to achieve a swift removal of them from the year 2000". New Zealand's stance starkly contrasts with Australia's decision last month to halt its unilateral reduction of automotive tariffs in 2005 at no lower than 15 percent.

Peters said the New Zealand way would be of greater benefit. "Removing remaining tariffs will benefit New Zealand exporters by reducing their costs, and will benefit New Zealand consumers by providing access to cheaper products."

Politically, the decision is far easier in New Zealand where only 1,800 people in four Japanese-owned companies are involved in car assembly whereas the Australian industry directly affects 47,000 jobs.
New Zealand has been running headlong down a path to free markets and removal of trade barriers since the mid-1980s.
The car industry here accepts it is doomed.
"If the tariff does go down to zero or towards zero, it makes it extraordinarily difficult to continue car assembly," said Mitsubishi Motors Corporate General Manager Rob Greenfield.
The industry has been shrinking since the 1970s when 14 assemblers protected by a 55 percent tariff and import licensing put together more than 90 percent of all new cars sold here.
"We would never expect a New Zealand government of the centre-right to go the Australian way because it is against what the trend has been. We are resigned to that," Greenfield said.
"The record of both the Australian Labor Party and the Liberal-National coalition is not as economically dry as their New Zealand counterparts have been," he said.

The four assemblers are local units of Honda Motor Co Ltd, Nissan, Mitsubishi Motors and Toyota Motor Corp. Together they sell about half of the estimated 60,000 annual new car registrations in New Zealand.
No decision has yet been made to abolish tariffs in 2000 following a review next year, but Peters and Commerce Minister John Luxton state that as their preferrence.
Luxton argues that since reducing tariffs in 1989, exports in affected industries have blossomed.

"We've had tremendous growth in our apparel area and these were people who 10 years ago could not survive without a tariff of 55 percent and import licensing to restrict other people coming in," he said.
But people in the industry suggest the baby may go with the bathwater. Apparel and Textile Federation chief executive Marcia Dunnett, said half of the 20,000 jobs in her industry would go.
While clothing exports had risen five-fold in eight years, exporters still needed a domestic base to work from, she said.
"The unseemly haste with which the government is... removing tariffs is agreed by observers to be extremely naive," said New Zealand Trade Union Federation Secretary Maxine Gaye.
"It takes no account of non-tariff protections that may be high in other countries but are very low in New Zealand."
The car assembly industry has spun off a NZ$200 million a year components export industry and spokesman David Tibby said the closure of assemblers could threaten 5,000 other jobs there.
